name: Tomas Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Tomas. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee assistant manager at Ridgeway Farms, a family business with about six hundred hectares of carrots, onions and wheat, plus a beef finishing unit of two hundred and fifty cattle. My day starts at seven with the crew briefing, then I walk crops with Mr Ridgeway's son, Andrew, check the cattle, and in the afternoon I sort the drone flights and the spray plans. Two years ago I was selling seed and fertiliser to farmers, so the field side is new to me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Slowly in the field, fast on the screens. I sold fertiliser to farmers for sixteen years, and now I'm the one who forgets to check the onion field for mildew. Andrew is patient. But I use AI every day, for the spray plans, the cattle weights, the staff rota, and that's why they pay me more than a normal farm hand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Isabel works part-time on reception at the dental surgery in town. Pablo's twelve and Marta's nine, they go to the Catholic school. We have a mortgage, savings for over a year, and my late father left me a twelve-hectare paddock that a neighbour rents for grazing. I believe in standing on your own feet, my father came here with one suitcase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said for years: it's a good tool, use it, but stop making it a religion. The farmers I used to sell to would agree. Hard work and good land still decide things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the same path. I learn the crops, one day Andrew runs the farm and I'm his right hand. My only real worry is that I'm still slow in the field, and last summer I missed mildew in the onions for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep using AI for the planning, it's already saving me an hour a day. Ask Andrew to give me my own field block next season, so I learn by doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually. It's a fine life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the onions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trusted the drone images and didn't walk the field. Andrew walked it and found the mildew in the low corner. It cost us part of a field and taught me to use my boots as well as my screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Pablo about AI in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use it like a calculator, but do the thinking yourself first. I make him do his maths homework without it.

say: AI is a **good tool**, but people should stop making it a religion.
**Hard work** and good land still decide things.
think: He stays on track to be **Andrew's right hand** at Ridgeway.
His worry is being **slow in the field**, like missing onion mildew.
do: **Keep** using AI for planning, saving an hour a day.
**Ask** Andrew for his own field block next season.
**Walk** the fields himself rather than trust drone images alone.
feel: **Calm** and content; it's a fine life.
S0.quote: I trusted the drone images and didn't walk the field. Andrew walked it and found the mildew in the low corner.
fieldNote: An ex-**fertiliser salesman** whose screen skills outpace his field skills.
Learned from **missed mildew** to walk crops as well as fly drones.
Strong cushion includes an inherited **grazing paddock**.

steps.text: Ask Andrew for his own field block at Ridgeway next season
Keep using AI for spray plans and the staff rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing, and farms that use it will win. I'd tell the lads at Ridgeway to learn it or fall behind. That's the market, and the market is fair in the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good. Ridgeway Farms is trialling a robot weeder this spring, and I want to be the man who knows it best. The part of my job that's planning and ordering would get faster. Isabel's reception job is the one that shrinks, because AI booking does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the robot weeder trial and write up the results for Mr Ridgeway. I'd move more of the ordering and rota work to AI tools. And I'd talk to Isabel about doing the books for the paddock and maybe a small business, so she isn't relying on the surgery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Some concern for Isabel, but my pay would go up, not down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Isabel say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Isabel said the surgery already has an online booking page and the phone rings less. Isabel isn't worried about the money, more about being bored at home. We'd find her something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market is fair. Fair to Isabel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair in the long run, I said. In the short run, it's hard on some people. That's what families and the parish are for.

say: Farms that use AI **will win**; learn it or fall behind.
The **market is fair** in the long run.
think: He wants to be the one who knows Ridgeway's **robot weeder** best.
Isabel's **reception job** shrinks as AI does bookings, though his pay rises.
do: **Run** the robot weeder trial and write up results.
**Move** ordering and rota work to AI tools.
**Help** Isabel start bookkeeping for the paddock.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with some concern for Isabel.
S1.quote: Ridgeway Farms is trialling a robot weeder this spring, and I want to be the man who knows it best.
fieldNote: He sees **thinking AI** as a boost to his management work.
Household risk is **Isabel's part-time** job, offset by his rising pay.
Admits the market is **hard short-term**, turning to family and parish.

steps.text: Run Ridgeway's robot weeder trial and write up results
Move ordering and staff rota work to AI tools
Help Isabel set up bookkeeping for the paddock rental

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest opportunity in a hundred years for anyone willing to work. I'd say don't wait for the government. I'd say that at church and in the farmers' group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my management work is the first thing to change in 2028, the planning and ordering AI does better than me. Then by 2031 robots do the field work. Isabel's job is gone. When everyone else is scared of the robots, that's when a man with savings should buy one and hire it out. That's my plan, but it's a risk with our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put half our savings into a robot weeder and set up a contracting business, hiring it out to smaller farms and using it on my paddock. Isabel would run the bookings and accounts. I'd keep my Ridgeway job as long as it lasts, nights and weekends on the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous. I'd be betting on myself, which I like, but it's the family's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the contracting business failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost half the savings and I still have the paddock and Isabel and the kids. I'd sell the robot second-hand. I'd rather try and lose than wait and lose anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doesn't your own job at Ridgeway worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. Andrew won't need a trainee manager if AI does the planning. But he'll need someone who runs the robots, and I'd make sure that's me until my business stands up.

say: This is the **biggest opportunity** in a hundred years for anyone willing to work.
think: His **management work** changes first, in 2028, as AI plans and orders.
Buying a robot while others are scared is a **risk** with family savings.
do: **Put** half the savings into a robot weeder.
**Start** a contracting business hiring it to smaller farms.
**Keep** his Ridgeway job as long as it lasts.
feel: **Excited and nervous**, betting the family's money on himself.
S2.quote: When everyone else is scared of the robots, that's when a man with savings should buy one and hire it out.
fieldNote: Unusually, his **thinking work** is more exposed than his hands-on work.
Sees fast AGI as a **business opening**, true to free-market views.
Accepts the **downside**: he'd rather try and lose than wait and lose.

steps.text: Put half the savings into a robot weeder
Hire the robot weeder out to smaller farms nearby
Have Isabel run the contracting bookings and accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's five years to get ahead, so get ahead. Learn, save, build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to build a robot contracting business before the big dealers notice the gap. By 2031 the thinking side changes my job, by 2034 the robots arrive in force. I'd have three good years of business before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start small: lease a robot weeder in 2029, test it on my paddock, then take on three or four farms. I'd keep saving until then, and learn the machines at Ridgeway first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and keen to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why lease rather than buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first robots will be expensive and out of date fast. Leasing lets me learn without losing the family's savings. Once it pays, I'd buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That their papa is starting a business, and that work is still work, even with robots. Pablo would want to come on the jobs.

say: There are **five years** to get ahead, so get ahead.
**Learn, save** and build something of your own while there's still a gap.
think: He can build a **robot contracting** business before big dealers move.
He'd get **three good years** of business before robots arrive in force.
do: **Lease** a robot weeder in 2029 and test it on the paddock.
**Take on** three or four farms as customers.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to build a robot contracting business before the big dealers notice the gap.
fieldNote: More time makes him **less risky**: lease first, buy later.
He frames the change for his children around the **dignity of work**, even with robots.

steps.text: Lease a robot weeder in 2029 and test it on the paddock
Sign up three or four nearby farms as contracting customers
Keep saving until the lease starts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who complains in 2036 had a decade to prepare. Work hard, learn the tools, don't expect handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a gift to anyone willing to work, and I'd make sure my children understood that. For me it's a clear road: manager at Ridgeway, then my own robot business. I'd be fifty-six in 2039, still young enough to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn every new machine at Ridgeway, keep using AI, save steadily. In five or six years, buy the first robot outright and start contracting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would bother you about ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone else has ten years too, so the competition is fiercer. The early bird gets more in the fast picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make sure Pablo and Marta understood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take them to work on Saturdays. Let them see the robot and the cattle and the books. Work is learned by watching.

say: **Ten years** is plenty; complaints in 2036 mean you ignored a decade.
Work hard, learn the tools, **no handouts**.
think: A **clear road**: manager at Ridgeway, then his own robot business.
With more time, **competition** for robot work gets fiercer.
do: **Buy** the first robot outright in five or six years.
**Take** Pablo and Marta to work on Saturdays.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift to anyone willing to work, and I'd make sure my children understood that.
fieldNote: Sees the long warning as **more competition**, not more safety.
Teaches the children work by **watching**, a traditional value.
His plan is unchanged across AGI pictures, only the **timing** moves.

steps.text: Learn every new machine Ridgeway brings in
Buy the first contracting robot outright within six years
Take Pablo and Marta to Ridgeway on Saturdays

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the biggest risk with our savings and my management work goes first. What would help is cheap business loans for farm robots and fewer rules on hiring them out, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people want to stand on their own feet. I do. Nobody owes me a living, but nobody's going to stop me earning one with a robot either.

headlineQuote: Nobody owes me a living, but nobody's going to stop me earning one with a robot either.
portrait: Ex-**fertiliser salesman**, now a trainee assistant manager on a large vegetable and beef farm.
Uses AI daily; his **thinking work** is more exposed than most farm jobs.
Strong savings and an inherited **paddock** give him room to take risks.
Calm in most pictures and only **uneasy** at AGI by 2028, which he treats as a business chance.
Plans a **robot contracting** business, with his wife running the books.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, the biggest risk with savings as his management work changes first.
whatWouldHelp: **Fewer rules** on hiring robots out, not handouts.
